title: Shubin v. William Lyon Homes, Inc.
lead: A hurried employment-signing process was procedurally unconscionable, but the historical appellate decision ordered arbitration after removing only a penalty on administrative proceedings.

actors.name: Kristy Shubin
actors.role: Employee alleging pregnancy and sex discrimination and harassment

actors.name: Kathy Sampson
actors.role: Office manager involved in signing the first agreement

actors.name: Justice Sepulveda
actors.role: Author of the unanimous appellate opinion

proceedings: Trial court denied the motion to compel arbitration.
Court of Appeal reversed and directed severance of “or administrative” and enforcement of the remainder.
California Supreme Court later directed omission of the opinion from the reporter.
limits: This is the historical November 14, 2000 decision, not currently published precedent: the Supreme Court ordered omission on March 14, 2001.
Discrimination allegations and the disputed first signing date were not resolved on their merits.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Shubin signs employment papers and later alleges discrimination
sections.cue: Introduce the relationship and the disputed signing process.
paragraphs: William Lyon Homes, Inc. hired Kristy Shubin as a receptionist in April 1998 and promoted her to escrow coordinator that December. In January 1999, she told Doug Bauer, president of its Northern California region, that she was pregnant. She alleged that Bauer and marketing/sales coordinator Connie Newbury reacted with hostility, that she was demoted, and that Bauer refused physician-required pregnancy accommodations in March. After obtaining a right-to-sue letter from California’s Department of Fair Employment and Housing, she sued in July for sex and pregnancy discrimination and harassment. The court did not decide whether those allegations were true.

The employer invoked a two-page employee agreement with an arbitration clause. Shubin said office manager Kathy Sampson had brought several papers to her desk late in the day, said headquarters needed signatures, stood beside her, and pointed out where to sign or initial. Asked what they were, Sampson allegedly called them hiring records and promised an explanation later. Shubin said she lacked time to read everything, felt unable to refuse, received no copies, and was not told she was agreeing to arbitration.

Sampson recalled giving her the agreement to read and sign, receiving no request for more time, and making no remembered promise of later explanation. Sampson placed signing on April 14, Shubin’s first workday; Shubin recalled roughly two weeks later. Her signature was undated, and William Lyon signed for the company May 18. The discrepancy remained unresolved.

sections.title: The employer invokes the clause after the administrative complaint
sections.cue: Follow the motion and the trial court’s objections.
paragraphs: In May 1999, after Shubin filed her administrative claim, another office manager asked her to sign another agreement. Requests to take it home, read it, consult counsel or obtain a copy were refused. The appellate court later treated that incident as corroboration of the company’s signing practices, not a substitute for proof about the original agreement.

The clause required an employment-law arbitrator chosen under JAMS/Endispute rules for employment or agreement disputes, expressly including discrimination and harassment. It excepted workers’ compensation, unemployment, taking or using confidential information, and claims under a confidentiality provision governing use during and after employment. Its last sentence allowed a responding party to recover costs, expenses and attorney fees if the other pursued a legal or administrative action over an arbitrable matter.

The company supplied a copy to Shubin’s lawyer with an August arbitration proposal. Counsel objected. In September, the employer moved to compel, arguing that discrimination was covered, ordinary remedies remained, limitations and discovery were not expressly curtailed, and exceptions benefited both sides. Shubin attacked the signing process, confidentiality carveout, incorporated deposition restrictions, arbitration costs and other-forum penalties.

The trial court denied arbitration October 8, finding unequal court access, discovery restrictions particularly harmful to the employee, and possible liability for the employer’s fees even if she prevailed elsewhere. Armendariz, the California Supreme Court’s later employment-arbitration decision, had not yet issued. The trial judge also apparently did not know that review of another cited decision, Maciejewski, had been granted two days earlier pending Armendariz.

sections.title: The appellate court preserves the procedural finding but construes statutory safeguards
sections.cue: Explain which defects were real and which interpretation addressed.
paragraphs: Justice Sepulveda, joined by Presiding Justice Hanlon and Justice Reardon, reviewed legal enforceability de novo, factual findings from declarations for substantial evidence, and a refusal to sever pervasive unconscionability for abuse of discretion.

The agreement was adhesive despite its brevity: a standardized employment condition without realistic negotiation. The duty to read did not dispose of the evidence. Rosenthal, an earlier fraud-in-execution decision, lacked comparable conduct pressuring a signer; Sampson’s alleged words and behavior supported a hurried process without meaningful reading or proposed changes. The trial court could credit Shubin. This established procedural unconscionability, not automatic invalidity of every unread employment form.

Applying Armendariz, the court found several protections implicit. Neutrality was unchallenged, and no unlawful restriction on statutory remedies was alleged. Agreement to arbitrate rights under the Fair Employment and Housing Act implied adequate discovery; incorporated JAMS default deposition rules did not expressly foreclose that construction. A written decision revealing essential findings and conclusions was also required, while the exact review standard was premature. The employer had to bear costs unique to mandatory arbitration; incorporating default cost rules did not specifically displace that obligation.

sources.pinpoint: Opinion parts II.A, II.D.1–5, II.E.1–3.a & nn. 5–7

sections.title: Only the administrative penalty requires removal
sections.cue: Connect mutuality and fee analysis to the narrow remedy.
paragraphs: The court rejected unequal access under this wording. Unlike Armendariz’s employee-only clause, the confidentiality exception did not expressly distinguish employer and employee. Though usually important to the employer, it also let an employee seek a declaration about permissible disclosure. Workers’ compensation and unemployment exceptions reflected statutory administrative processes rather than employer concessions.

For a contractual court action, Civil Code § 1717 made fee recovery bilateral and dependent on prevailing, defeating the reading that a successful employee must pay a losing employer. But that statute did not appear to govern administrative proceedings. An employee properly bringing a discrimination complaint before the state agency could still incur the contractual penalty. Armendariz preserved that access, and the chilling penalty was substantively unconscionable to that extent.

Removing “or administrative” from the last sentence cured the sole substantive defect without adding obligations or impairing the agreement’s purpose. Armendariz had involved multiple defects and nonmutual scope requiring rewriting; this clause did not. On November 14, 2000, the Court of Appeal reversed and directed that deletion and enforcement of the remainder. Procedural unconscionability alone had not defeated arbitration, and the discrimination merits remained unresolved.

The California Supreme Court subsequently ordered the opinion omitted from reporter pages 1041–1063 on March 14, 2001. The account therefore describes that historical appellate ruling, not a currently published precedent.

sources.pinpoint: Opinion parts II.E.3.b–c, II.F, III & n. 8; reporter omission notice
